title: How could one man write a dictionary? | SAMUEL JOHNSON

entries.note: Lichfield-born bookseller's son (1709) who left Oxford, married an older woman in Derby, and became famous as 'Dictionary Johnson' after his 1755 [[see:A Dictionary of the English Language]].

entries.term: A Dictionary of the English Language
entries.note: Johnson's 1755 dictionary: two folio volumes, 42,773 words and about 114,000 quotations, the first to pair definitions with usage examples and commentary.

entries.term: A Short Scheme for Compiling a New Dictionary of the English Language
entries.note: Johnson's 1746 plan for his dictionary, aiming to 'fix' the English language, an ambition he later abandoned.
[[see:Robert Cawdrey]]'s 1604 list of about 2,400 hard words, often seen as the first dictionary but more like a vocabulary book.
[[see:Nathan Bailey]]'s 1721 dictionary of 40,000 words, broader than earlier works but lacking literary depth and consistent structure.
A [[see:ghost word]] in a much later dictionary, created when slips reading 'D or d' (for density) got mixed up.
A word that should not be in the dictionary, such as [[see:dord]], [[see:foop]] and [[see:adventine]].
Johnson's ghost word 'to drive with sudden impetuosity', from a [[see:William Camden]] quotation, probably a misread long S in [[from?:soupe]].
The likely real word behind [[see:foop]], related to [[see:swoop]], and also no longer in use.
A ghost word, a misprint for [[from:adventive]] in a quotation from [[see:Francis Bacon]].
Another ghost word from misreading [[see:Francis Bacon]], meant to refer to tooth cutting.
Johnson's famous definition calls a writer of dictionaries a [[see:harmless drudge]].
Johnson's description of a [[see:lexicographer]], which lexicographers today happily use for themselves.
Johnson's entry includes the example that compiling dictionaries is dull work.
Johnson admitted 'of this word I know not the meaning'.
Johnson first wrote 'I know not the meaning', but by the fourth edition defined it as a species of red colour.
Another word Johnson admitted he didn't know the meaning of, and the hosts think nobody does.
Called by Johnson a barbarous contraction of [[from:awkward]], meaning odd or out of order; it sounds like 'orcs'.
Johnson called it an unnecessary word creeping into the language, as he disliked French borrowings.
Another French borrowing Johnson hated.
A French word meaning a sort of memory, which Johnson was glad had fallen out of use.
Johnson's label for ordinary words he disliked, perhaps because people below his class used them, though sometimes clearly meant as a sneer.
Called by Johnson a low word with no settled meaning; it then meant manual rather than intellectual dexterity.
Johnson approved of it as a word for good things (as in crack shot), and also recorded it as low language for a prostitute.
An odd opinion-related word Johnson said was tried in different forms but 'not yet received, nor is it wanted'.
Johnson called it a vile word, a ludicrous reduplication of [[from:twattle]].
Called a low word by Johnson; it replaced [[see:wideness]] and was formed on the model of [[see:breadth]] and [[see:depth]].
The preferred word before the 1700s, later displaced by [[see:width]].
One of the models on which [[see:width]] was formed.
One of the models on which [[see:width]] was formed.
Discussed in the grammar episode; a modern shift probably modelled on 'on purpose', compared with the formation of [[see:width]].
The older form that [[see:on accident]] is shifting away from, mentioned from the grammar episode.
Johnson called it a barbarous corruption of [[from:less]], formed by the vulgar habit of ending comparatives in -er.
Johnson's joke definition: food for horses in England and for people in Scotland, possibly teasing his Scottish assistants.
Defined by Johnson as a man of artifice, or one of deep contrivance.
Johnson called it a cant term, probably derived from an Irish word meaning a savage.
Johnson defined it simply as the name of a faction, though elsewhere he mocked Whigs (see [[see:leader]]).
Johnson's example sentence reads 'the detestable Wharton was the leader of the Whigs', a dig at the [[see:Whig]] party.
Johnson told an old lawyer joke: he wouldn't speak ill of any man behind his back, but believed the gentleman was an attorney.
Defined as a wretch who supports with insolence and is paid with flattery, a dig after Johnson fell out with [[see:Lord Chesterfield]].
Johnson's patron, whose praise Johnson found condescending, leading to a public falling-out reflected in the [[see:patron]] entry.
Covered in the weird jobs episode; an inspector of beer purity, whose post Johnson called a sinecure for decayed citizens.
Johnson defined it as the cheat of foretelling fortune by the lines of the palm.
Johnson defined it as a buffoon who practises gesticulations.
Defined as pay to a state hireling for treason, which backfired when Johnson accepted a £300 pension from [[see:George III]].
Johnson's 'hateful tax' definition so offended the Commissioners of Excise that they considered suing but decided against it.
Johnson called it a woman's word, cant among women for anything unpleasing.
From the same source as [[same-root:chant]], Latin [[from:cantus]]; possibly tied to beggars repeatedly chanting appeals for alms.
Shares its Latin source, [[from:cantus]], with [[same-root:cant]], as in religious chants and songs.
Another word Johnson labelled women's cant.
One of many insulting words for women, defined by Johnson as a decayed strumpet.
Johnson defined it as a pert young hussy.
Originally a word for a dog, later in Johnson a young, pert, wanton girl.
Johnson called it a personal satire meant to vex a particular person, distinct from general [[see:satire]], and said people confused them.
In Johnson, proper satire is marked by the generality of its reflections, unlike a [[see:lampoon]].
Johnson said [[see:Matthew Prior]] barbarously clipped it from [[from:hypercritic]] without knowing what the word meant.
In Johnson, one more critical than necessity requires; the source of [[gave:hyper]].
Johnson mocked [[see:Junius]], who 'with his usual idleness of conjecture' derived it from Greek.
Johnson linked it to a Welsh word it almost certainly doesn't come from.
A variant of [[same-root:scramble]]; Johnson mocked [[see:Meric Casaubon]]'s failed attempts to explain its origin.
From the Latin for prayer, meaning dependent on another's will; Johnson complained that people misused it to mean simply uncertain.
In Johnson's dictionary it wasn't specific to girls; a boy could be a tomboy too.
Johnson defined it as a philologer or grammarian, someone interested in words.
As a noun Johnson defined it as a rude, awkward, boisterous, untaught girl.
Before it was a shoe, Johnson defined it as a large vessel of drink.
Johnson gave it a negative sense: essentially a liar.
Now flattering, but Johnson defined it in negative terms.
Now flattering, but Johnson defined it in negative terms.
Johnson defined it as civility involving some hypocrisy; an etymological doublet of [[same-root:complement]], reshaped via Italian and disliked by him.
Johnson said this was the proper form, meaning something superfluous or more than enough; a doublet of [[same-root:compliment]].
Means secret or clandestine, from Latin [[from:clanculum]], a diminutive of Latin [[see:clam (Latin)]]; Johnson defined it using the harder word [[see:clandestine]].
Loosely related to [[same-root:clancular]] and used by Johnson to define it.
Latin for secretly, which gave the diminutive [[gave:clanculum]]; the 14th-century English interjection may refer to it.
Relatively modern slang that pictures a clam shutting its shell.
In 14th-century English an interjection meaning be quiet, possibly from Latin; the sea creature's name is unrelated to Latin [[unrelated:clam (Latin)]].
Johnson defined it with no fewer than 12 synonyms.
Johnson gave it a 750-word explanation.
Coined by [[see:Alexander Pope]] to match [[see:talkative]]; Johnson called it 'a word of Pope's, not to be imitated'.
Thinking of a clever remark after a conversation; the hosts prefer it to [[equivalent:staircase wit]] because it needs no explanation.
The usual term for [[equivalent:after-wit]], though it always needs explaining.
Defined by Johnson as a secret enemy who pretends to be a friend.
One who professes friendship without meaning it, similar to [[see:backfriend]].
A frequently cited entry meaning eructation tasting of undigested roast meat: a meat burp; its root means steam, fumes or food aroma.
Classical Latin word for someone who loves the smell of cooking, sharing a root with [[same-root:nidorosity]].
A parasite who haunts good tables, drawn by [[see:nidorous]] smells; Rob suggests it for teenagers who appear only at mealtimes.
Meaty-smelling, used in a description of the [[see:smell-feast]]'s attraction to banquets.
Producing or bearing ducks, from Latin [[from:anas]], duck, plus -fer, carrying; Johnson's quotation links it to the [[see:barnacle goose]].
A figure in medieval bestiaries, behind the trees in the [[see:anatiferous]] quotation; the hosts save its whole story for another episode.
Medieval bestiaries, which the hosts call wild, prompted by the [[see:barnacle goose]], and they suggest an episode on them.
A trinket, knick-knack or slight contrivance in machinery; Johnson tolerated it, unlike [[see:twittletwattle]].
Johnson noted it cannot be pronounced without making the noise it means, as with many onomatopoeic words like [[see:lisp]].
Like [[see:hiss]], a word that performs the sound it names.
Defined by Johnson as in a state of desire, from Old French [[from:en gogues]], in good humour; perhaps influenced by [[see:aghast]] and [[see:agape]].
Often paired with [[see:agog]], and possibly influenced its meaning.
Another word often paired with [[see:agog]], possibly influencing its meaning.
Johnson's word for a contractor of words, someone who shortens them; compare [[same-root:syncopation]].
Musical syncopation, likened to [[same-root:syncopist]].
Johnson defined it as private men's opinion differing from that of the Catholic and Orthodox church.
Johnson's entry praises escaping popish ways, showing his hostility to Catholics.
Like [[see:Reformation]], defined by Johnson in terms celebrating escape from popish ways.
Previously covered by the hosts; Johnson proposed [[from?:non compos mentis]] as its origin, which is probably wrong, and nobody really knows.
Johnson's suggested, probably incorrect, origin of [[see:nincompoop]].
Johnson wrongly derived it from French for a wicked heart; it may come from 'corn merchant', but more likely from a Gaelic word for a disagreeable person.
A word worth reviving, meaning serpent-eating.
An adjective meaning covered with a hat.
A stupid fellow or dolt, one of the self-explanatory words worth reviving.
In Johnson, a foolish or insignificant person.
Not a happy thought but the forked bone of fowls, a [[see:wishbone]], named for the game where the longer piece foretells who marries first.
The modern word for what Johnson called a [[see:merrythought]].
